source: Heander, Soderberg, Rydenfalt (2025) Code Review as Decision-Making
finding: Think-aloud study of code review finds the process maps onto Klein's RPD model: an orientation phase (like recognition) then an analytical phase.
numbers: 10 participants, 34 code reviews, one national software company; thematic, statistical, temporal and sequential analysis.
limits: Single company, small N. The RPD mapping is the authors' interpretation, not a test against a rival model.
agent_relevance: Review tasks for our agent can follow the same two steps: orient and recognise the change type first, then analyse.

source: Heander, Soderberg, Rydenfalt (2025) Code Review as Decision-Making
finding: They map orientation to the preparatory half of RPD (experience the situation, recognise) and the analytical phase to a full RPD cycle with mental simulation of code and team behaviour.
numbers: Output is the CRDM model with decision points: write comment, seek info, vote, run locally, check CI.
limits: Model is descriptive. No outcome measure of review quality.
agent_relevance: Gives named decision points where S0 quick mode could stop or escalate.

source: Heander, Soderberg, Rydenfalt (2025) Code Review as Decision-Making
finding: Paper restates Klein (1998) RPD: no listing of all options; take the first action that mental simulation says will work, modify or discard it, move on.
numbers: Fig. 4 reproduces the RPD flow: experience, recognise (goals, cues, expectancies, actions), simulate, modify, implement.
limits: Secondary restatement, not the 1986 data.
agent_relevance: Matches a satisficing, first-workable-option loop with a simulation check.

source: Lin et al. (2023) SwiftSage: fast and slow thinking agent
finding: SwiftSage pairs a small fine-tuned fast module (770M) with a GPT-4 planner. It beats SayCan, ReAct and Reflexion on ScienceWorld.
numbers: 30 task types. Average score 84.7 vs SayCan 33.8, ReAct 36.4, Reflexion 45.3; SWIFT-only agent 49.22.
limits: Fast module needs oracle trajectories for training. Reflexion got up to 4 rounds, others 1, so comparison is uneven. One benchmark.
agent_relevance: Direct template for S0 quick mode: act fast by default, hand off to deliberation on trigger.

source: Lin et al. (2023) SwiftSage: fast and slow thinking agent
finding: Rule for switching from fast to slow: stuck, invalid action, critical decision, unexpected observation. This is the RPD violated-expectancy trigger in code.
numbers: Switch when K=5 steps give zero reward, or the proposed action is invalid, or it is a critical decision, or an exception appears. Revert when the action buffer empties.
limits: Hand-set heuristic; K=5 not tuned in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Copy the four triggers as S0 exit conditions.

source: Lin et al. (2023) SwiftSage: fast and slow thinking agent
finding: Fast default is also cheaper because the big model is called only when needed.
numbers: 757.07 tokens per action vs SayCan 1,855.84, ReAct 1,971.03, Reflexion 2,983.46.
limits: Token cost only; no wall-clock.
agent_relevance: Quick mode saves cost as well as time.

source: Lin et al. (2023) SwiftSage: fast and slow thinking agent
finding: Fast module alone cannot handle exceptions (broken stove); plan-and-ground prompting in the slow module does.
numbers: SWIFT-only 49.22 vs full 84.7 overall.
limits: Qualitative example.
agent_relevance: Recognition fails on novel exceptions; keep a deliberate fallback.

source: Meneses dos Santos & Oliveira (2026) Cognitive extensions for dual-process language agents
finding: Adding execution-time validation (self-reflection) to SwiftSage helps most; episodic memory helps less alone.
numbers: Mean final score baseline 51.67, +AMM 53.83, +SRM 64.33, full 64.62; success 23.99%, 26.94%, 41.33%, 43.17%; steps to success 24.48 to 19.33.
limits: Local Qwen2.5-7B runtime, not SOTA; one benchmark (ScienceWorld).
agent_relevance: Check the fast action before it runs (a mental-simulation gate); this was the biggest gain.

source: Meneses dos Santos & Oliveira (2026) Cognitive extensions for dual-process language agents
finding: With the checker on, slow-system calls fall and fast-path steps rise.
numbers: Buffer-executed steps 55.92% to 37.99% in one table row; System 2 calls 24.6 to 14.1 per episode; long tasks: AMM alone -6.6%, SRM +21.0%.
limits: Details from a tabular text extraction; some cells may be misaligned.
agent_relevance: A good fast path plus validation can cut slow calls by about 40%.

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) NDM-inspired prompts for LLM triage, JMIR Biomed Eng
finding: Only source found that tests Klein-style prompts on LLMs: RPD and data-frame prompts raised accuracy over a default prompt on patient triage.
numbers: Per search summary: 6 ChatGPT models, 45 vignettes, 10 runs each; overall 63.3% default, 67.6% RPD, 66.7% data-frame; self-care 13.4% to 29.8% with RPD.
limits: Page could not be fetched; numbers come from a search summary only and need checking. Preprint reported 70.2% vs 64.7%. Narrow care-seeking task.
agent_relevance: If it holds, an RPD-style prompt is a cheap lever, mostly on the under-triage class.

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) NDM-inspired prompts for LLM triage, JMIR Biomed Eng
finding: Authors say effect on real user decisions is untested.
numbers: Not available.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on it until read in full.

source: Rivera et al. (2024) Escalation risks from language models in military and diplomatic decision-making
finding: Eight LLM nation agents in a turn-based wargame all escalate, with sudden hard-to-predict jumps, arms races and rare nuclear use.
numbers: 5 models (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude 2, Llama-2-70B-Chat, GPT-4-Base); 3 scenarios; significant initial escalation for all models; no significant de-escalation; GPT-3.5 score rose 10.15 to 26.02 (+256%) in neutral scenario.
limits: Simulated, not experts; one prompt family; old models. Not RPD-specific.
agent_relevance: Fast LLM action choice without a failure check drifts to escalation; add a pre-commit check on high-stakes actions.

source: Rivera et al. (2024) Escalation risks from language models in military and diplomatic decision-making
finding: Models justified escalation with deterrence and first-strike reasoning in their chain of thought.
numbers: Qualitative; chain-of-thought collected per action.
limits: Reasoning text may not reflect the true cause of the action.
agent_relevance: Chain of thought is not a safeguard by itself.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs machine: expert humans and LLMs in wargames
finding: 214 national-security experts vs LLM-simulated teams in a US-China crisis: high-level agreement, but LLMs differ in individual actions and can be more aggressive.
numbers: N=214 experts; models GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4o and others; simulated dialog of 3 rounds brought aggressiveness closer to human for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.
limits: Fictional scenario; teams are simulated by one model.
agent_relevance: LLMs approximate average expert choices but not expert variation.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs machine: expert humans and LLMs in wargames
finding: LLMs ignore player traits: no significant difference even when told players are strict pacifists or aggressive sociopaths.
numbers: No significant difference on both moves for all models.
limits: Test of persona prompting only.
agent_relevance: Role prompts do not install an expert's experience-based recognition.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized planning with large-scale transformers: grandmaster-level chess without search
finding: A 270M transformer trained on Stockfish 16 labels plays by pattern recognition with no test-time search: grandmaster-level.
numbers: Lichess blitz Elo 2895 vs humans; puzzle Elo up to 2867; 10M games annotated.
limits: Distilled from a search engine; perfect distillation not reached. Blitz humans may be weaker than classical.
agent_relevance: Strongest machine case of 'experts see the move' (chunk recognition) without search.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized planning with large-scale transformers: grandmaster-level chess without search
finding: Recognition only works when training covers the domain; scale and data matter.
numbers: Ablations over dataset size, model size and target type.
limits: Domain is closed and fully labelled.
agent_relevance: S0 recognition is only as good as the stored cases; open domains need escalation.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2022) Thinking fast and slow in large language models
finding: Early GPT-3 models give human-like intuitive answers and errors on cognitive-reflection items; ChatGPT and GPT-4 avoid them.
numbers: CRT-type tasks: GPT-4 96% correct, ChatGPT-3.5 59%, GPT-3-davinci-003 5%, humans 38%. Intuitive errors 80% davinci, 55% humans, 15% ChatGPT-3.5, 0% GPT-4.
limits: Replication check: CRT 38% vs 41% in original (n=3,428). Old models. Reading from text extract.
agent_relevance: Strong models are rarely 'intuitive' in the trap sense, so quick mode should be judged by cost, not by mimicry.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2022) Thinking fast and slow in large language models
finding: Chain-of-thought moves GPT-3 away from intuition; blocking it hurts only slightly in GPT-4.
numbers: Davinci: correct 5% to 28%, intuitive 80% to 29% with CoT. Blocking CoT in GPT-4: correct 95% to 88%, intuitive 0% to 10%.
limits: Small task set.
agent_relevance: Strong models carry much of the 'slow' work in their weights, so quick mode can be safe on familiar items.

source: Kim et al. (2025/2026) InvThink: premortem reasoning for safer language models
finding: Prompt or train the model to list failure modes before answering (a pre-mortem). It cuts harm more than 'be safe' instructions.
numbers: Harmfulness 3.22 zero-shot to 2.19 (-32.0%); SafetyPrompt 2.62; blackmail rate -90%, murder attempts -44% (prompting); SFT+RL gave 0 harmful actions in 100 trials per seed.
limits: Does not cite Klein by name in what I read; judged by LLM ensemble; single seed on reasoning evals.
agent_relevance: Pre-mortem step is a tested operator; place it in the S0-to-slow handoff for risky actions.

source: Kim et al. (2025/2026) InvThink: premortem reasoning for safer language models
finding: Reasoning benchmarks are not hurt and may improve with the pre-mortem training.
numbers: Up to +5.0% on GPQA and MATH500, +2.0% MMLU (SFT+RL variant); gains largest on open-ended ethics tasks.
limits: Authors flag it as suggestive, not significant.
agent_relevance: Low cost to the agent's accuracy.

source: Liptay et al. (2026) Evaluating strategic reasoning in forecasting agents (Bench to the Future 2)
finding: Better AI forecaster differs mainly by doing a pre-mortem of its blind spots and considering black swans.
numbers: 1,417 pastcasting questions; 15M-document frozen corpus; detects 0.004 Brier gaps; built forecaster is 0.011 Brier better than any single frontier agent.
limits: One period (Oct-Dec 2025); geopolitics and economics heavy; observational analysis of traces.
agent_relevance: Supports pre-mortem as the habit that separates strong forecasters.

source: Liptay et al. (2026) Evaluating strategic reasoning in forecasting agents (Bench to the Future 2)
finding: Human experts found frontier agents fail at modelling leaders' incentives and treating stated positions as commitments.
numbers: Qualitative case studies.
limits: Few cases.
agent_relevance: Agents lack the situation model that RPD experts use for expectancy checks.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) DPT-Agent: dual process theory for real-time human-AI collaboration
finding: A fast finite-state-machine and code-as-policy layer plus slow reasoning beats ReAct and Reflexion in real-time Overcooked-style play.
numbers: Rule-based partners: overall score ReAct 15.48, Reflexion 11.77, DPT-Agent about 44-47; 71 university students in human tests.
limits: Column labels in the text extract are scrambled; exact order of the two DPT scores uncertain. One game.
agent_relevance: When latency matters, a fixed fast policy beats a thinking-heavy loop.

source: Dualformer: controllable fast and slow thinking by learning with randomized reasoning traces (2025)
finding: One model trained on randomly shortened reasoning traces can run in fast, slow or auto mode.
numbers: Maze 30x30: slow 97.6% optimal vs Searchformer 93.3% with 45.5% fewer steps; fast mode 80% vs solution-only 30%; auto 96.6% with 59.9% fewer steps.
limits: Maze and math only; authors not read.
agent_relevance: Auto mode is a learned S0 gate; a prompt-only gate is the cheaper version.

source: Mainali et al. (2025) Classical AI vs LLMs for decision-maker alignment in health insurance choices
finding: Older AI decision systems explicitly use naturalistic decision making next to case-based and Bayesian methods; LLM versions match them on alignment.
numbers: Risk targets 0.0, 0.5, 1.0; GPT-5 and GPT-4 with weighted self-consistency; classical slightly better at the moderate profile.
limits: Alignment to attribute targets, not outcome quality; sample sizes not extracted.
agent_relevance: NDM-style case models are a precedent, but LLM zero-shot already matches them.

source: Klein, Calderwood, Clinton-Cirocco (1986) Rapid decision making on the fire ground (via secondary pages)
finding: Founding fireground study: commanders mostly used recognition, not option comparison.
numbers: About 80% of decisions examined, per a blog summary; simulation rarely used more than three factors.
limits: Secondary source, not the paper; later critics argue interview recall bias.
agent_relevance: Use the number only as a rough anchor; open the paper before citing.

source: Skill-style web pages on RPD for agent design
finding: Several web pages propose RPD-based agent designs but give no tests.
numbers: None.
limits: Opinion pieces; no measurements.
agent_relevance: No evidence yet that an RPD scaffold beats plain prompting beyond Kopka and Feufel.
